titel: The business model and risks of banks
kurz: How banks work with maturity transformation and leverage, why this gives rise to banking crises and how deposits and securities are protected.

bloecke.md: A bank's business is based on different maturities. On the liabilities side there is money that customers can withdraw at any time. On the assets side there are claims that run for ten, twenty or thirty years. This conversion of short-term deposits into long-term claims is called [[maturity transformation]]. It is indispensable for the economy, because nobody could finance a house if loans could only run as long as the longest savings deposit. At the same time, it is the weak point from which every banking crisis arises. Regulation, capital buffers and insurance can limit this risk, but not eliminate it.

bloecke.titel: Stylised balance sheet of a European universal bank (illustrative calculation, total assets normalised to 100)
kopf: Liabilities and equity (who it belongs to)

bloecke.md:
The table is best read from the bottom right. There, six units of equity support a hundred units of assets. If the assets side loses 6% of its value, the owners' capital is used up in arithmetical terms. An industrial company with an equity ratio of 30% or 40% can absorb a 6% loss in value without major problems, but for a bank the same loss always threatens its existence. High leverage is part of the business model. The interest margin between deposits and loans is only a few percentage points, and only leverage turns this into an adequate return on equity.

The second weak point lies in the maturity of the deposits. The bank is 74% funded by customer deposits. For the bank they are a source of funding; for customers they are legally a claim, most of which is payable on demand. The claims on the assets side, by contrast, cannot be called in at short notice. The bank cannot demand early repayment of a ten-year mortgage loan. Bonds can be sold, but only at the day's market price and not at their acquisition cost.

bloecke.md:
## Rising interest rates and book losses

There has been a rise in interest rates of this magnitude. The yield on ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) averaged minus 0.51% in 2020 and 2.43% in 2023. That is a rise of around three percentage points in three years. Every bank that had bought long-dated securities in 2020 subsequently recorded book losses. They only become real losses when the bank has to sell the securities. This is the difference between default risk and interest rate risk. A security can be one hundred per cent safe and still lead to ruinous losses.

bloecke.titel: Yield on ten-year Bunds, annual averages
bloecke.unter: The yield rose from minus 0.51% (2020) to 2.61% (2025). The turnaround in 2022 triggered all the book losses that arose on bank balance sheets in this cycle.

bloecke.md:
Silicon Valley Bank (SVB) had total assets of $209 billion and deposits of around $175 billion. Around nine tenths of these were above the limit of US deposit insurance. More than $150 billion was therefore not protected by deposit insurance in an emergency and would only have been repaid pro rata from the proceeds of the resolution. The assets side consisted largely of long-dated government and mortgage bonds from the low interest rate period. At the end of 2022 there were more than $15 billion of unrealised losses on the books.

The losses of $15 billion corresponded to 7.2% of total assets of $209 billion. The bank's equity stood at $15.5 billion, just over 7% of total assets, and was therefore almost completely wiped out in economic terms, even though the balance sheet still looked solid. The reason was that securities held to maturity did not have to be valued at market prices. On 9 March customers withdrew $42 billion, around a quarter of all deposits, in a single day. The following day the bank was closed. Signature Bank followed on 12 March and First Republic on 1 May.

## The logic of a bank run

Customers who withdraw first get their money at face value. Those who come last only get the residual value of a balance sheet whose assets were sold in distress. This is why even customers who consider the bank sound withdraw their money as soon as they expect others to do so. This behaviour is not herd instinct but the equilibrium response to a payout rule based on the principle of *first come, first served*. This is how it is described in the model by Diamond and Dybvig, for which the Nobel Prize in Economics was awarded in 2022.

What is new is the speed. In the past, a run meant a queue forming outside the branch, and opening hours and cash holdings limited the outflows. Today a run consists of online banking transfers, triggered by a chat among business customers. SVB's $42 billion flowed out within hours. At Credit Suisse the outflows dragged on for longer, but were no smaller. In the fourth quarter of 2022 alone, CHF 110.5 billion left the bank, followed by a further CHF 61.2 billion in the first quarter of 2023. On 19 March 2023 UBS took over the bank, which had been founded in 1856, for three billion Swiss francs in shares. The share price had been above CHF 90 in 2007 and fell as low as CHF 1.55 during trading on 15 March 2023.

## Two capital ratios

For regulatory purposes, capital is measured against [[risk-weighted assets]] and not against total assets. A loan to a medium-sized business counts in full, while a German federal bond counts as zero under the standardised approach. Basel III requires Common Equity Tier 1 capital of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets. In addition, there is a capital conservation buffer of 2.5 percentage points, countercyclical and systemic buffers, and institution-specific add-ons set by the supervisor. Alongside this, the unweighted leverage ratio applies, under which total Tier 1 capital, including Additional Tier 1 capital (AT1), must reach at least 3% of total assets plus off-balance-sheet exposures. It is deliberately designed to be crude and takes effect in cases where models set a risk at zero. In the EU, the final Basel rules have applied since 1 January 2025 through CRR III (Capital Requirements Regulation). This includes an output floor that gradually brings the results of internal models closer to the standardised approach.

The model bank from above has 6 units of common equity (CET1) and 100 units of total assets. After risk weighting, this results in 38 units of risk-weighted assets.

- The CET1 ratio is 6 / 38 = 15.8%. That looks like a large cushion and is far above any minimum requirement.
- The leverage ratio is 6 / 100 = 6.0% if only CET1 capital is counted. That looks thin. Including the AT1 portion of the subordinated capital, it comes out slightly higher.

Both figures are correct. The first shows how well the bank is protected against the risks that the model captures. The second shows how much loss in value it can absorb if the model is wrong. At SVB, the bonds that brought it down carried almost no weight after risk weighting.

## Deposit protection

In the EU, deposits of up to €100,000 are protected by law, in Germany through the Deposit Guarantee Act (Einlagensicherungsgesetz). The limit applies *per customer and institution*. Two accounts at the same bank are therefore added together, a joint account counts separately for each holder, and banks in the same group can share the same banking licence. Payment is made within seven working days, without the need to submit an application.

bloecke.md: These protection schemes are organised nationally. A common European deposit protection scheme has been under discussion since 2015, but has not materialised to this day. The banking union therefore has only two pillars instead of three. Instant-access savings at a bank in another EU country are also protected by law there up to €100,000. In an emergency, however, payment depends on the solvency of the local protection fund, and these funds are equipped to varying degrees relative to the total assets of the national banking sector.

## Bail-in and the order of liability

After 2008, legislators changed who bears the losses of a banking crisis. Until then, banks in crisis had been propped up with capital from tax revenue. Since the European Bank Recovery and Resolution Directive, implemented in Germany in the Recovery and Resolution Act (Sanierungs- und Abwicklungsgesetz), the [[bail-in]] rule has applied. Under it, the bank's capital providers bear the losses first, in a fixed order. Only when at least 8% of total assets have been drawn on in this way may the Single Resolution Fund step in. For the model bank above, that is eight out of a hundred units and therefore almost everything that equity and subordinated capital, with nine units together, can provide. This is why banks must also hold bonds that are eligible for bail-in.

bloecke.unter: The ranking runs from top to bottom; at the top are the capital providers who are liable first. Covered deposits at the base are exempt from bail-in.

stufen.text: Shareholders. Liable in full and first.

Specially created class that is liable before the rest of the debt capital.

bloecke.md: At Credit Suisse, AT1 bonds worth CHF 16 billion were written down in full on 19 March 2023, while the shareholders still received something through the share exchange. This reversed the usual ranking. FINMA based the write-down on the bond terms and on Swiss emergency law. In October 2025 the Swiss Federal Administrative Court declared it unlawful, because the contractual trigger had not occurred and the emergency law did not provide a sufficient legal basis. The ruling is not final; FINMA and UBS have lodged an appeal with the Swiss Federal Supreme Court. For buyers of subordinated bonds or certificates, it follows that the ranking is governed by the prospectus and cannot be derived from intuition. Which bank is rescued at all is, moreover, a political decision. In 2008 Bear Stearns and AIG were propped up, but Lehman Brothers was not.

## Deposits and securities accounts

The most important practical distinction in banking is the one between a claim and ownership. Money in a current account is a claim against the bank, and this claim is only as good as the bank itself. Securities in a securities account are different. The customer remains the owner or co-owner of the collective holding, the securities are held by a central securities depository, and if the bank becomes insolvent they do not form part of the insolvency estate. They are segregated and transferred to another institution. For fund units, there is a second layer of protection. The fund's assets are held as [[segregated fund assets (Sondervermögen)]]; they are separate from the assets of the fund management company, and its creditors have no access to them.

punkte: Property of the customer, not a claim against the bank
Does not fall into the insolvency estate; it is segregated
Fund units additionally protected as segregated fund assets
No limit on the amount; even a portfolio worth €500,000 is fully protected
The residual risk is misappropriation, for which investor compensation of up to €20,000 is available

bloecke.md:
- Spread amounts above €100,000 across several institutions, and check whether two brands belong to the same banking licence.
- After a property sale or a severance payment, the increased protection only applies for a limited period of six months.
- Do not leave large cash balances in the settlement account permanently. Money market funds are segregated fund assets; instant-access savings are not.
- With high interest rate offers from other European countries, check which protection fund pays in an emergency as well as the interest rate.

With a high share of borrowed funds, a bank is betting that not all customers will demand their money back at the same time and that the assets side will retain its value. Regulation reduces the probability that this calculation does not work out, but does not eliminate it. It also shifts the costs of failure from the taxpayer to the bank's capital providers.

begriffe.text: The bank's business of converting deposits available at short notice into long-term loans. This gives rise to the interest margin and at the same time to the liquidity and interest rate risk that underlies every banking crisis.

The basis for calculating capital ratios under Basel. Each exposure is multiplied by a risk weight, government bonds often by zero under the standardised approach. The denominator is therefore smaller than total assets and depends on the model used.

Participation of a bank's capital providers in its losses in a legally fixed order before public funds may be used. At least 8% of total assets must be drawn on in this way before the resolution fund steps in.
